Freight rate prediction, end to end

The result in one line. A CatBoost regressor on a log target predicts freight rates to $114.99 MAE and 5.03% MAPE on data it has never seen — a 90.0% error reduction against a constant-rate baseline and 20.8% against the best linear model.

What actually mattered

The problem is extrapolation

Training ends 2025-10-31; scoring begins 2025-11-01. Zero overlap. A random split would have measured the wrong thing entirely — this single fact drove the split, the date encoding and the feature set.

Distance is the price

Three distance features carry over 90% of model importance (r = 0.909). Everything else — equipment, geography, market — is a modifier on top of the mileage.

The tail dominates the error

Median absolute error is $54.30 against a mean of $114.99. The worst 1% of loads carry 39.3% of all error — which is why RMSE barely moved across six model families.

Every model evaluated

Project Overview

From inherited repository to delivered submission

The project began as an audit of an existing codebase and ran through nine phases to a scorer-validated submission.

Business problem

Given a load's lane, equipment type, weight, date and market context, predict the rate it will post at. Accurate pricing lets a broker quote competitively without eroding margin.

The cost of a mispriced load is approximately linear in dollars, which is why MAE is the headline metric throughout rather than RMSE — RMSE would be dominated by a handful of very high-rate loads that no model predicts well.

What the inherited repository got wrong. The audit found a swallowed exception in the preprocessing runner that had silently renamed all 142 processed feature columns to integers — feature names were being destroyed with no error raised. It also found a broken import structure, an incomplete requirements.txt that produced a non-functional environment, and a missing December input file that made one deliverable impossible. Phase 3 repaired all four.

Approach

  • Audit before building. Nothing was assumed about the inherited code; every claim was verified against the data.
  • Evidence over convention. Each cleaning and modelling decision is backed by a measurement — see the Decision Log.
  • Structural correctness. Leakage prevention and feature-name preservation are enforced by assertions, not by discipline.
  • Honest reporting. Where the evidence is weak — the model-selection margin, the flat December curve — the dashboard says so rather than overselling.
Dataset

48,000 labelled loads, 12,000 to predict

Two disjoint time windows — the single most important structural fact about this problem.

Target. posted_rate is strictly positive and right-skewed: median $2,031, mean $2,374, max $25,533. That skew is why a log target helps, and why the back-transformation needed a bias correction.

Phase 1 · Data Audit

Four material quality issues, each verified

Nothing was cleaned on suspicion. Each repair is justified by a measurement that distinguishes a data fault from a real signal.

IssueEvidenceResolution
292 negative weight valuesMean of |negative| = 31,724 vs positive mean 31,415; both span an identical [5,000, 47,500] range — a sign-flip fault, not a distinct population.Repaired with abs(), then clipped.
Missing weight / market_index300 / 374 in train (0.63% / 0.78%), but 1.38% / 2.08% in validation — the rate roughly doubles.Median imputation plus explicit missingness indicators.
8 unseen pickup citiesAllentown, Charlotte, Chicago, Jackson, Knoxville, Laredo, Norfolk, San Diego — present only at scoring time, affecting 725 rows (~6%).Explicit *_is_unknown flags; geography carried by coordinates.
Degenerate temporal featuresdate_year constant (2025); date_month is {11,12} at scoring vs {1..10} in training — outside the model's learned support.Replaced with cyclical day-of-year / day-of-week encodings.
The most dangerous finding was in the code, not the data. The inherited preprocessing runner wrapped get_feature_names_out() in a bare try/except with a silent fallback. The call was failing on every run, so all 142 processed columns were written with integer names — feature names were lost entirely and nothing reported an error. This is now guarded by assert_feature_names_preserved(), which fails loudly on any integer or placeholder column name.
Phase 2 · Exploratory Analysis

What drives a freight rate

Five findings that shaped every subsequent decision.

Distance is the price

corr(distance, posted_rate) = +0.909. It explains the overwhelming majority of rate variation.

Rate-per-mile falls with distance

r = −0.335. Short hauls spread fixed costs over fewer miles, so a flat $/mile quote is wrong at both ends.

Equipment carries a real premium

Median $/mile: Dry Van 2.115, Flatbed 2.295 (+8.5%), Reefer 2.383 (+12.7%).

Pricing is directional

corr(delivery_lon, rate) = −0.257 — a westbound premium a single distance scalar cannot express.

Market context is weaker than it first appears. Daily mean market index correlates +0.577 with daily mean $/mile — but that is co-movement of averages, not sensitivity. The measured elasticity is only 0.139: a 1% rise in market index moves rate-per-mile by 0.14%. This distinction later explained the shape of the December chart.

Rate-per-mile by distance band

Median $/mile falls monotonically as hauls lengthen.

Rate-per-mile by equipment

Reefer commands the largest premium over Dry Van.

Phase 3 · Feature Engineering

156 named features

Deliberately narrow. Every engineered feature is justified by a measurement, and names survive end-to-end so nothing is anonymous downstream.

Categorical (one-hot) 131

delivery_Albany, delivery_Albuquerque, delivery_Amarillo, delivery_Atlanta, delivery_Austin, delivery_Bakersfield, delivery_Baltimore, delivery_Baton Rouge, delivery_Birmingham, delivery_Boston, delivery_Buffalo, delivery_Charleston, delivery_Chattanooga, delivery_Cincinnati…

bearing_cos, bearing_sin, delivery_lat, delivery_lon, haversine_miles, lat_delta, lon_delta, pickup_lat, pickup_lon

Why cyclical time. doy_sin/cos and dow_sin/cos are bounded in [−1, 1] and continuous across the year boundary, so November and December never leave the support the model was trained on. A monotone day counter was explicitly disabled for the opposite reason.
Phase 3 · Preprocessing Pipeline

Stateless first, fitted last

The ordering is the design: if every learned statistic lives in one stage, the leakage audit reduces to inspecting that stage.

Raw feature frame
13 columns from CSV
↓
RawDataCleaner
Weight sign repair & clip; whitespace strip. Row-local, so it cannot leak.
↓
FeatureBuilder
Temporal, geospatial, interaction and indicator features. Schema frozen at fit.
↓

Median, learned from training rows only

Robust for weight, standard elsewhere
One-hot
131 columns; unknowns flagged separately
↓
156 named features
Verified: no integer names, no NaNs, train/inference aligned
Stateless — no fitted state Fitted — learns from training rows only Output

Integrity guards

  • assert_feature_names_preserved() — fails if any column name is an integer or an sklearn placeholder. The direct regression guard for the inherited bug.
  • assert_frames_aligned() — train and inference columns must match in content and order.
  • assert_no_missing_values() — no NaN may survive preprocessing.
  • assert_no_leakage() — neither the target nor load_id may reach the feature matrix.
  • An independent refit must reproduce the feature matrix exactly.

An honest caveat on the margin. CatBoost, LightGBM and HistGradientBoosting sit within $4 of each other on a $2,280 mean prediction — inside fold-to-fold noise. CatBoost is the defensible pick, but it should be read as one of three near-equivalent models rather than a decisive winner.
Why HistGradientBoosting rather than GradientBoosting. scikit-learn documents the exact-split GradientBoostingRegressor as far slower for n_samples ≥ 10,000. With 38,477 training rows and 156 features it would have dominated the phase runtime for no accuracy benefit, so the histogram implementation was used instead.

Read the RMSE column. It varies by barely 2% across every model tried, while MAE spans $115–$1,149. RMSE simply cannot discriminate between these models, because it is dominated by a tail that none of them predicts. That is a finding about the data, not a deficiency in any model.
Phase 6 · Explainability

Three methods, one conclusion

Native importance, permutation importance and SHAP each have a different blind spot, so all three are reported. Where they disagreed, the disagreement was the finding.

Reading the numbers. The model predicts log(rate), so importances and SHAP values live in log-dollar space. Contributions are additive in logs, which means multiplicative in dollars: a SHAP value of +0.10 is roughly a +10.5% effect on the rate, not +$0.10.

Top 20 features

Switch between CatBoost's in-sample score and out-of-sample permutation importance. Hover for both ranks and the feature's rationale.

Method
The market_index discrepancy is informative. It ranks 7th on CatBoost's native score but only 15th out-of-sample, with a permutation effect two orders of magnitude below the distance features. Its measured elasticity is 0.139. An earlier draft of this analysis described market context as the dominant operational signal; the permutation evidence contradicted that, and the claim was corrected rather than left standing.
Phase 6 · Error Analysis

The tail is the whole story

Measured on 9,523 genuinely unseen loads. Sign convention: a positive residual means the model under-priced the load.

DiagnosticMeasurementVerdict
Heavy tailsExcess kurtosis 265; worst 1% of loads carry 39.3% of all absolute errorDominant
HeteroscedasticityResidual SD varies 4.24× across prediction quintiles; corr(|residual|, prediction) = 0.115Present
Systematic biasMean residual +$101.81 (t = 15.69)Corrected
Why RMSE never moved. Across six model families RMSE stayed pinned between $636 and $654 while MAE ranged from $115 to $1,149. Every model shares the same heavy tail — a minority of loads priced by mechanisms not present in these features. No hyperparameter fixes that, and it is the single largest remaining opportunity in the project.
Phase 6 · Business Insights

What a pricing desk should do with this

Six recommendations, each traceable to a measurement rather than intuition.

1 · Quote uncertainty as a percentage

Residual spread varies 4.24× across prediction quintiles. A flat ±$X band is far too wide on cheap loads and far too narrow on expensive ones.

2 · Never quote a flat $/mile

Rate-per-mile falls monotonically with distance (r = −0.335). Use the banded figures as a sanity check on any manual quote.

3 · Refresh market context daily

It is the dominant time-varying input, so a stale market_index degrades every prediction that day at once — though the effect size is modest (elasticity 0.139).

4 · Route the tail to human review

Error is concentrated enough that a queue covering the worst ~1% of loads captures roughly 39% of total error — a small manual workload for a large risk reduction.

5 · Treat Nov–Dec as extrapolation

No labelled data exists for the scoring months. Monitor realised rates against predictions weekly and be prepared to recalibrate.

6 · Collect data for the 8 unseen cities

Allentown, Charlotte, Chicago, Jackson, Knoxville, Laredo, Norfolk and San Diego are currently priced from geography alone.

The smearing correction

MetricUncorrectedCorrectedChange
MAE$132.15$114.99−13.0%
RMSE$641.48$636.25−0.8%
MAPE5.68%5.03%−0.65 pp
Tested before adoption, not assumed. Smearing targets the conditional mean while MAE is minimised by the conditional median — the two genuinely conflict, so adopting it blind would have been a coin flip. It was evaluated on the untouched holdout using the already-fitted Phase-5 model, which cost no extra training. All three metrics improved, so it was adopted (factor 1.0128).

Submission validation

Phase 7 · December Analysis

Why the curve is nearly flat — and why that is right

A fixed lane — Lexington to Fort Wayne, 360 miles, Dry Van, 32,000 lb — across all 31 days of December, with only the date changing.

Rows

Predicted rate across December 2025

Only the date changes. Hover for the exact predicted rate on any day.

This narrow range is the correct result, not a defect — and it was worth verifying rather than assuming. Across these 31 dates the market index swings +25.8% (0.831 → 1.045). The elasticity measured directly from the data is 0.139, which implies a rate response of only +3.2%. The model produces +2.7% — closely tracking the data. On a lane with fixed mileage, equipment and weight, date is genuinely a minor price driver in this dataset.
The visible weekly rhythm — mid-week peaks, weekend troughs — comes from the cyclical dow_sin/dow_cos features. Had the inherited raw date_month encoding been kept, this chart would have been a flat line: every December date would have fallen into the same out-of-range leaf.
Reference · Decision Log

14 engineering decisions, with the evidence behind each

Every non-obvious choice in the project: why it was made, what else was considered, and what it changed. Expand any row.

FoundationalTime-based split instead of a random split
Decision
Hold out the final contiguous block of the development window (2025-09-01 to 2025-10-31) rather than sampling rows at random.
Why
Training data ends 2025-10-31 and scoring begins 2025-11-01 with zero overlap. The task is forward extrapolation, so a random split would measure interpolation skill the model will never be asked to use.
Alternatives
Random k-fold; grouped split by lane; a single random holdout.
Evidence
The two windows are strictly disjoint. Every fold was verified to train only on rows earlier than the rows it scores.
Impact
All reported metrics are honest forward-in-time estimates. This was the single most consequential decision in the project.
FoundationalLeakage prevented structurally, not by convention
Decision
Make preprocessing a step inside the searched pipeline so scikit-learn clones and refits it independently within every CV fold.
Why
Fitting the preprocessor once on all training data leaks future feature distributions into earlier folds. Relying on discipline to avoid this fails silently and is invisible in the metrics.
Alternatives
Fit once and reuse (faster, but leaks); manual per-fold refitting (correct but easy to get wrong).
Evidence
verify_no_leakage() asserts fold ordering and disjointness; assert_no_leakage() confirms neither the target nor load_id reaches the feature matrix.
Impact
No imputation median, scaler statistic or one-hot vocabulary is ever learned from data later than the rows it scores. Costs runtime, buys correctness.
FoundationalCyclical date encoding, and no monotone time feature
Decision
Encode date as doy_sin/cos and dow_sin/cos. Drop date_year and raw date_month; explicitly disable days_since_reference.
Why
date_year is constant (2025) and carries zero information. Raw date_month takes values {11, 12} at scoring against {1..10} in training — tree models cannot extrapolate and collapse both scoring months into the October leaf. A monotone day counter has the same defect.
Alternatives
Raw month/day integers (the inherited implementation); one-hot months (same failure); a linear time trend.
Evidence
Training months {1..10} vs scoring {11, 12}, verified from both CSVs. Cyclical encodings are bounded in [-1, 1] and never leave the training support.
Impact
Removes the extrapolation failure mode entirely, and produces the weekly periodicity visible in the December chart.
Data qualityNegative weights repaired by sign flip, not discarded
Decision
Apply abs() to 292 negative weight values, then clip to the observed envelope [5,000, 47,500].
Why
The absolute values of the negative population are distributionally identical to the positive population, identifying a sign-flip data-entry fault rather than a distinct physical population.
Alternatives
Drop the rows (loses usable data); treat as missing and impute (discards a recoverable true magnitude); leave as-is (corrupts the scaler).
Evidence
Mean of |negative| = 31,724 vs positive mean 31,415; both span an identical [5,000, 47,500] range.
Impact
Recovers 292 usable rows with their true magnitudes intact.
Data qualityMissing-value indicators alongside imputation
Decision
Emit weight_is_missing and market_index_is_missing before median imputation.
Why
Missingness rates roughly double between training and scoring. Imputing without flagging would silently hide a real distribution shift from the model.
Alternatives
Impute silently; drop rows; model-based imputation.
Evidence
weight missing 0.63% train vs 1.38% validation; market_index 0.78% vs 2.08%.
Impact
Two extra features; the model can condition on the fact of missingness.
Data qualityExplicit unknown-category flag over frequency bucketing
Decision
Keep handle_unknown='ignore' and add explicit *_is_unknown flags rather than bucketing rare categories.
Why
With plain one-hot, an unseen city becomes an all-zero vector indistinguishable from 'no city at all' — the encoder fails silently by design.
Alternatives
min_frequency bucketing was measured and rejected: the lowest workable threshold collapses 14 of 64 genuine cities to catch unknowns.
Evidence
8 cities appear only at scoring time, affecting ~6% of scoring rows. Coordinate features remain fully informative for those rows.
Impact
Preserves all 64 city identities while making the unknown state learnable.
ModellingLog target chosen on measured evidence
Decision
Train every advanced model on log(posted_rate) via TransformedTargetRegressor.
Why
The target is right-skewed (median $2,031, mean $2,374, max $25,533). Log training also guarantees strictly positive predictions after inversion, which the scorer requires.
Alternatives
Identity target; Box-Cox; square-root.
Evidence
In Phase 4 the log-target Ridge beat identity Ridge on MAE ($145.24 vs $149.36) and MAPE (6.27% vs 8.65%).
Impact
Better MAE and structural positivity, at the cost of the back-transformation bias addressed below.
Highest impactDuan smearing correction, tested before adoption
Decision
Rescale predictions by the mean of exponentiated training residuals (factor 1.0128).
Why
A log-target model fitted to the conditional mean of log(rate) returns the conditional median after exp(), which sits below the mean for a right-skewed target. Phase 6 measured the resulting bias at +$101.81 (t = 15.69).
Alternatives
No correction (accept the bias); a parametric log-normal correction, which assumes normal residuals — the QQ plot rejects that assumption.
Evidence
Evaluated on the untouched holdout before adoption, because smearing targets the conditional mean while MAE is minimised by the median — the two genuinely conflict. Here they did not: MAE $132.15 → $114.99, RMSE $641.48 → $636.25, bias $101.81 → $73.37.
Impact
A 13.0% MAE improvement for one multiplication. The factor is strictly positive, so positivity cannot be violated.
Within noiseCatBoost selected — with an explicit caveat
Decision
Select CatBoost on holdout MAE from five tuned advanced models.
Why
Lowest holdout MAE and MAPE of every model evaluated.
Alternatives
LightGBM ($135.78) and HistGradientBoosting ($136.21) are effectively tied; RandomForest and XGBoost were clearly behind.
Evidence
CatBoost $132.15 vs LightGBM $135.78 — a $3.63 gap on a $2,280 mean prediction, which is inside fold-to-fold variation.
Impact
A defensible pick, but one of three near-equivalent models rather than a decisive winner. Reporting it otherwise would overstate the evidence.
ModellingMAE as the headline metric, not RMSE
Decision
Rank and select every model on holdout MAE.
Why
The business cost of a mispriced load is roughly linear in dollars. RMSE is dominated by a small number of very high-rate loads no model predicts well.
Alternatives
RMSE; R²; MAPE.
Evidence
RMSE varied only $640–$654 across six model families while MAE spanned $132–$158 — RMSE could not discriminate between them.
Impact
Selection tracked genuine differences in typical-load accuracy.
EvaluationHoldout-first evaluation, scored once
Decision
Tune with cross-validation on the training block only; score the holdout once per model and never tune against it.
Why
Repeatedly consulting a holdout turns it into a training set and inflates the final estimate.
Alternatives
Select on CV score alone; iterate against the holdout.
Evidence
CV and holdout rankings genuinely disagreed (RandomForest CV $167.68 → holdout $144.85) — exactly the information a contaminated holdout would have destroyed.
Impact
The reported $114.99 MAE is an honest estimate rather than an optimised one.
EvaluationThree independent explainability methods
Decision
Report CatBoost native importance, permutation importance and SHAP together.
Why
Each has a different blind spot: native is in-sample and over-credits high-cardinality splits; permutation is out-of-sample but under-credits correlated features; SHAP is additive but splits credit between them.
Alternatives
Native importance alone — the common shortcut.
Evidence
The disagreement was itself the finding: market_index ranks 7th natively but 15th by permutation, with a measured elasticity of 0.139.
Impact
Prevented overstating market context as a driver, and explained the shape of the December chart.
EngineeringStateless-first pipeline architecture
Decision
Order the pipeline as cleaning → feature construction → encoding, with all fitted state confined to the final ColumnTransformer.
Why
If every learned statistic lives in one stage, the leakage audit reduces to inspecting that stage. Scattered fitted state cannot be reasoned about.
Alternatives
A monolithic transformer; cleaning outside the pipeline (the inherited approach, which risks train/inference divergence).
Evidence
Integrity guards assert feature-name preservation, column alignment, no residual NaNs, and exact reproducibility on refit.
Impact
Training and inference are provably identical, and the December path reuses the same object rather than duplicating logic.
RecoveredReconstructing the missing December input file
Decision
Rebuild data/december_chart_inputs.csv from the constants in score.py, and reconstruct the six columns its schema omits.
Why
The file the scorer requires was absent from the inherited repository, making the second deliverable impossible to produce.
Alternatives
Skip the deliverable; guess the scenario.
Evidence
score.py pins pickup, delivery, distance, equipment, weight and the date range exactly. Coordinates come from a verified city lookup (exactly one coordinate pair per city); market context from a per-date table covering all 31 December dates, all inside the training range.
Impact
Unblocked the deliverable with an exact rather than approximate reconstruction.

Derived artifacts are git-ignored and fully regenerable. processed/, models/ and scorer_results/ can all be rebuilt from the raw CSVs with a fixed seed — with one deliberate exception: candidate_december.png is force-tracked because it is a required submission artifact.

Reference · Model Card

CatBoost freight rate regressor

Metadata, training procedure, inputs and outputs, performance, failure modes and deployment considerations.

Model details

AlgorithmCatBoost regressor
Targetlog(posted_rate), inverted with exp
Back-transformDuan smearing, factor 1.0128
Hyperparameterslearning_rate: 0.03, l2_leaf_reg: 1.0, iterations: 400, depth: 6
Features156 engineered
Random seed42

Training procedure

Training rows48,000
Window2025-01-01 → 2025-10-31
SelectionRandomised search, 3 expanding-window folds
Selection metricHoldout MAE
Final fitExactly one run on the full window
Leakage controlPreprocessing refit inside every fold

Inputs

  • Categorical: pickup, delivery, equipment
  • Numeric: origin/destination lat-lon, distance, weight, market_index, quote_signal
  • Temporal: date
  • Accepts a raw DataFrame — preprocessing lives inside the persisted pipeline

Outputs

  • A single predicted_rate in USD per load
  • Guaranteed finite and strictly positive — log inverse, a positive smearing factor, and an explicit floor
  • Observed range on the scoring set: $201.65 – $6,465.66
  • No prediction interval is produced — see limitations

Performance

On 9,523 loads from 2025-09-01 to 2025-10-31, never seen during fitting or tuning:

$114.99MAE
$636.25RMSE
0.8262R²
5.03%MAPE
$54.30Median abs. error

Known failure modes

  • High-rate outliers. The worst 1% of loads carry 39.3% of total error; the single worst is off by $16,364. These loads are priced by mechanisms not present in the features.
  • Unseen cities. 8 cities appear only at scoring time and are priced from coordinates alone. The *_is_unknown flag makes the state explicit but cannot recover missing lane history.
  • Far-future dates. Cyclical encoding keeps predictions in-support, but the model has no mechanism for a genuine regime change beyond the observed market range.
  • Stale market context. A missing or outdated market_index degrades every prediction for that day simultaneously.

Deployment considerations

  • Persisted as a complete pipeline — no separate preprocessing step to keep in sync.
  • Single-threaded inference on 12,000 rows completes in under a second.
  • Quote uncertainty as a percentage, not a dollar band (heteroscedasticity confirmed).
  • Route the top ~1% by predicted rate to human review to absorb tail risk.
  • Monitor market_index drift and realised-vs-predicted error weekly.
Reference · Deployment Readiness

8 of 11 dimensions production-ready

An honest assessment. The modelling and reproducibility story is complete; the operational story is not, and is scoped rather than glossed over.

DimensionStatusDetail
ConfigurationReadyAll paths, column roles, split dates and feature switches live in config/config.yaml. No hardcoded literals in the pipeline.
LoggingReadyCentral logger.py; every stage emits structured progress. No bare print() in library code.
ReproducibilityReadyGlobal seed 42 across random, numpy and PYTHONHASHSEED. An independent refit is asserted to reproduce the feature matrix exactly.
TestingReady93 tests covering config, cleaning, features, pipeline integrity, splitting and inference. ruff clean.
Model persistenceReadyComplete pipeline serialised to models/final_model.joblib with a metadata record (seed, hyperparameters, metrics, smearing factor).
DocumentationReadyREADME, 9-page technical report PDF, 11 markdown reports, and this dashboard.
Prediction pipelineReadyBoth the full and reduced-feature paths converge on the same fitted object; verified end-to-end against the official scorer.
Submission artifactsReady12,000-row CSV and the December chart, both scorer-validated.
MonitoringNot builtNo drift detection or realised-vs-predicted tracking exists. Required before production use.
Prediction intervalsNot builtHeteroscedasticity is confirmed, but the model emits a point estimate only.
Serving layerNot builtNo API, container or batch scheduler. The model is a library artifact, not a service.
What “not built” means here. The three gaps are deliberate scope boundaries, not oversights. This was assessed as a modelling exercise with a fixed submission format; monitoring, prediction intervals and a serving layer are the first three items any real deployment would need, and they are listed so the gap is explicit rather than discovered later.
Conclusion

What was built, and what it is worth

A reproducible, leakage-free pipeline delivering a scorer-validated submission — with its weaknesses stated as plainly as its results.

Final MAE
$114.99
out-of-sample
vs constant baseline
−90.0%
error reduction
vs best linear
−20.8%
error reduction
Scorer
Passed
exit 0

What went well

  • The split reflects the real task. Recognising the forward-extrapolation structure early drove the holdout design, the cyclical date encoding and the decision to avoid monotone time features. A random split would have produced flattering numbers that collapsed at scoring time.
  • Correctness is enforced, not assumed. Leakage prevention is structural; feature-name preservation, column alignment and determinism are asserted on every run. The inherited bug that silently destroyed all feature names cannot recur.
  • Decisions were tested, not assumed. The smearing correction could have hurt MAE — it was measured on the holdout before adoption and delivered a 13% improvement.
  • Claims were corrected when evidence contradicted them. Market context was initially described as the dominant operational signal; permutation importance and a measured elasticity of 0.139 said otherwise, and the analysis was revised.

What remains open

  • The heavy tail is unresolved and is the single largest remaining opportunity. RMSE is 5.5× MAE and did not respond to any model family tried. Quantile regression or a two-stage normal/exceptional classifier is the natural next attempt.
  • The model-selection margin is within noise. Three models sit within $4; presenting CatBoost as a decisive winner would overstate the evidence.
  • Nov–Dec performance is inferred, not measured. No labelled data exists for the scoring window, so the $114.99 figure is carried forward from Sep–Oct.
  • Operational tooling does not exist — no monitoring, intervals or serving layer.
The through-line. The work’s main strength is that its conclusions are measured rather than assumed. The two findings most likely to be misread — the near-flat December curve and the weak market_index effect — were investigated and explained rather than presented at face value or quietly smoothed over.
